title: Selling to Different Decision-Makers
subtitle: One product, four audiences — how to adapt your message for users, managers, executives, and buyers
description: The same product needs to be described completely differently depending on who you are talking to. Users want to know if it will make their day easier. Managers want to know if their team will actually adopt it. Executives want to know if it moves a strategic number. Buyers want to know if it is worth the risk and the spend. Giving the wrong message to the right person — or the right message to the wrong person — is one of the most common reasons good deals stall. This lesson teaches how to read your audience, adapt your language, and make the same value land differently in every room.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley realises mid-conversation that she has been using executive language with a manager — and resets in real time

vocabulary.definition: Anyone with an interest in or influence over a purchasing decision. In complex B2B sales, a deal typically involves multiple stakeholders — users, managers, executives, and buyers — each with different priorities and different definitions of success. Failing to identify all of them is one of the most common reasons deals stall after a strong initial conversation.
vocabulary.example: Riley had been speaking exclusively to Marcus for three meetings — and only in the fourth meeting did she discover that the CFO, the Head of IT, and two senior users were all stakeholders in the decision. Each of them needed a different version of the conversation she had been having with Marcus alone.

vocabulary.definition: A defined profile representing a type of decision-maker — based on their role, their priorities, what success looks like for them, and what they are most afraid of. Different personas require different language, different metrics, and different emotional appeals, even when the product being described is identical.
vocabulary.example: Riley built a one-page persona map before the multi-stakeholder meeting: the CFO persona was focused on ROI and risk; the Head of IT persona was focused on integration and security; the senior users persona was focused on learning curve and whether the tool would actually save them time. Same meeting, three fundamentally different conversations.

vocabulary.definition: A person inside the prospect's organisation who advocates for your solution internally — attending meetings you are not in, answering questions you cannot hear, and building the internal case on your behalf. Identifying and equipping a champion is often more important than the quality of the external pitch, because the internal conversation is the one that actually determines most decisions.
vocabulary.example: Marcus had become Riley's champion without either of them using the word. He was forwarding her emails to the CFO, repeating her arguments in meetings she was not invited to, and flagging the competitor threat in his weekly report. Riley's job was to give him the language, the data, and the story he needed to do that effectively.

vocabulary.definition: Return on Investment — the financial return generated by a decision relative to its cost. Executive and buyer audiences require a credible ROI conversation before approving a significant purchase. The ROI must be specific, defensible, and expressed in terms the audience already uses to measure success — not in terms the vendor has invented.
vocabulary.example: When Riley met the CFO, she did not talk about features or workflow improvements. She talked about ROI: the average time-to-value for accounts of similar size was eleven weeks, the efficiency gain translated to approximately 880 freed hours per month across the team, and the cost of the contract was recovered — at conservative assumptions — within one quarter. The CFO asked two follow-up questions. That was when Riley knew the number was right.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which a new tool, system, or process becomes genuinely embedded in an organisation's daily workflow — not just purchased, but actually used. Manager and user audiences care about adoption more than executives, because they are the ones who have to make it happen. A solution that is bought but not adopted is, from the organisation's perspective, a failed investment.
vocabulary.example: The Head of Sales had approved three tools in the past two years that had never reached full adoption — bought by the executive team, resisted by the users, and eventually abandoned. When Riley spoke to the team leads, she spent more time on the onboarding experience and the support structure than on the ROI. Adoption was the conversation they needed to have before the one about results.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity to affect a decision or outcome without having formal authority over it. In complex B2B sales, influence often matters as much as authority — the senior user who tells the VP the team will never use this can kill a deal the CFO has already approved. Mapping influence, not just hierarchy, is what separates experienced from inexperienced salespeople.
vocabulary.example: The Head of IT had no formal authority over the purchasing decision — but his opinion on security and integration carried significant weight with the CTO, who did. Riley spent forty-five minutes with the Head of IT on a call that no one told her she needed to have. Three days later, the concern about data compliance disappeared from the conversation.

vocabulary.definition: Agreement reached across multiple people or perspectives. In complex B2B sales, decisions often require consensus among stakeholders who have different, sometimes competing, priorities. The salesperson's job is not just to convince each individual — it is to understand how those individuals will reach agreement with each other, and to make that process easier.
vocabulary.example: The deal was stalling because the CFO and the Head of Operations had different views on the implementation timeline. Neither was wrong — they just had different constraints. Riley did not try to convince one of them to change their position. She proposed a phased implementation that gave the CFO the financial structure she needed and gave Operations the preparation time they required. Consensus was not a compromise — it was a redesign.

vocabulary.definition: The specific statement of value or benefit being offered to a particular audience. In a multi-stakeholder sale, the proposition must be adapted for each decision-maker — the same features become different benefits depending on who is listening. A proposition that works perfectly for a VP of Sales will usually fail completely with a CFO, even when the underlying product is identical.
vocabulary.example: Riley prepared four versions of her proposition for the multi-stakeholder meeting. For the users: you will spend less time on the parts of your job that are not actually your job. For the manager: your team will onboard new clients in three days instead of fourteen. For the CFO: the investment is recovered within one quarter at conservative assumptions. For procurement: the contract includes a service level agreement with financial penalties for downtime above 0.1%.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT DOES SUCCESS LOOK LIKE FOR YOU
phrasalVerbs.definition: The universal opening probe for any new stakeholder — surfaces what they actually care about before you assume it from their job title. A CFO and a VP of Sales in the same company may define success in completely different terms, and getting this wrong means delivering the right answer to the wrong question.
phrasalVerbs.example: Before I walk you through how this works, I want to make sure I understand what success looks like for you specifically — because the Head of Sales and the CFO have described it quite differently, and I want to make sure this conversation is useful for your role rather than a repeat of one you have already had.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: IN YOUR ROLE, WHAT MATTERS MOST IS
phrasalVerbs.definition: A persona-specific framing device — signals that you have adapted your message to the person in front of you rather than delivering a standard pitch. It also invites correction: if your assumption about what matters to them is wrong, they will tell you before you have spent twenty minutes on the wrong thing.
phrasalVerbs.example: In your role as Head of Operations, what matters most is probably whether your team can actually adopt this without disrupting the quarter — not whether the ROI model holds up on paper. So I want to start there, rather than with the number I showed the CFO.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: THE WAY YOUR TEAM WOULD FEEL THIS IS
phrasalVerbs.definition: The translation phrase for user and manager conversations — converts features and business metrics into day-to-day experience. Users do not think in ROI; they think in time, frustration, and workflow. The way your team would feel this puts the value in terms they can evaluate from their own experience.
phrasalVerbs.example: The way your team would feel this in the first month is: the Friday afternoon report that currently takes three hours gets done automatically overnight. That is not an efficiency gain on a slide — that is three hours back, every week, for every person on the team.

phrasalVerbs.definition: The pivot phrase for executive conversations — signals that what follows is about strategic impact, competitive position, or financial return, not product features or day-to-day workflow. Executives do not buy tools; they buy outcomes. From a business perspective is the signal that you are about to speak their language.
phrasalVerbs.example: From a business perspective, the question is not whether the tool saves time — it does. The question is whether that time translates into measurable revenue impact. At similar companies, the freed capacity has been redirected to pipeline activity, and the average result is a 12% increase in deals advanced per rep per quarter.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR BUDGET IS
phrasalVerbs.definition: The buyer and procurement frame — translates value into the financial and risk terms that purchasing and finance audiences need to evaluate. Procurement does not care that the sales team will be more productive; they care about total cost of ownership, contract risk, vendor stability, and whether the investment is defensible.
phrasalVerbs.example: What this means for your budget is a fixed annual cost with no variable charges, a service level agreement with financial penalties for any downtime above 0.1%, and a standard data processing agreement that your legal team can approve without custom negotiation. I want to make the procurement process as straightforward as possible.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHO ELSE NEEDS TO SEE THIS
phrasalVerbs.definition: A stakeholder-mapping probe — surfaces other decision-makers or influencers without making the current person feel their authority is being questioned. Phrased as a process question rather than a challenge, it positions you as someone trying to help the deal succeed rather than someone trying to go around the person in front of you.
phrasalVerbs.example: Before we move to next steps — who else needs to see this, or be part of the conversation? I want to make sure the right people have what they need, and I would rather map that now than discover a missing conversation three weeks from now when we are trying to close.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Riley, I have to be honest — I have enjoyed our conversations, but when you talk about strategic alignment and revenue impact, it does not quite connect for me. I am a Head of Sales Operations. I care about whether my team can actually use this.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That is a really useful piece of feedback — and I appreciate you saying it directly. I have been giving you the executive [[proposition:the specific statement of value adapted for a particular audience]] when what you need is the operations conversation. Let me reset. In your role, what matters most is probably whether this actually gets [[adopted:embedded in daily workflow rather than just purchased]], not whether the ROI model holds up on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Exactly. I have seen three tools bought at exec level in the last two years that my team never actually used. I am the one who has to manage the fallout from that.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That is the most important thing you have told me. The way your team would feel this in the first month is: the Friday afternoon report that currently takes three hours gets done automatically overnight. That is not an efficiency gain on a slide — that is three hours back, every week, for every person on the team. The question is whether they believe it will actually work, or whether they will resist it the way they resisted the last two tools.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That is exactly the question. How do I prevent another failed adoption?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: The answer is in how we structure the rollout — not the product itself. We start with two or three of your most senior users, people whose opinion carries [[influence:the capacity to affect a decision without formal authority]] in the team. If they adopt it and say it works, the rest of the team follows. If we start with the whole team at once, the first friction point becomes the story everyone tells.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I like that approach. But I also need to manage upward. My CFO will ask me to justify the spend and my CEO is going to want to know what the strategic case is.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Those are different conversations that need different language. For your CFO, the conversation is about [[ROI:Return on Investment — the financial return relative to cost]]: the investment is recovered within one quarter at conservative assumptions, and the contract includes penalty clauses for downtime so the financial risk is bounded. For your CEO, the conversation is about competitive position — from a business perspective, two companies in your sector started this in Q3 and are already in the compounding phase of the efficiency gain.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: So I need three different conversations. That is a lot to manage internally.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That is exactly where I can help you. You are the [[champion:someone inside the organisation who advocates for a solution internally]] here — and my job is to make sure you have everything you need to have each of those conversations without me in the room. I can prepare a one-page summary for the CFO in her language, a brief for your CEO that uses the competitive framing, and a rollout proposal for your team leads that addresses the adoption concern directly.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That would actually be very useful. Who else do you typically need to speak to in organisations like ours?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: In most deals this size, we find there are four [[stakeholder:anyone with interest in or influence over a decision]] groups: the user team, the operations lead — which is you — the executive sponsor, and procurement. We have covered two of those today. The one I would want to add, based on what you have told me about the previous failed tools, is two of your senior users — directly, before the broader rollout conversation. Their voice shapes the team's perception more than any top-down announcement.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Who else needs to see this — other than the CFO, CEO, and the senior users?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Procurement will need to see the contract and the SLA, and IT will want to review the data handling. Neither of those is a blocker if we get ahead of them — they become blockers if we surface them at the end. I would like to send IT the technical documentation this week, before anyone asks for it. That way, by the time [[consensus:agreement across multiple stakeholders]] is needed, the process conversations are already done and only the decision conversation is left.

registerAwareness.context: Opening a conversation with a user-level stakeholder
registerAwareness.example: I want to make sure this conversation is useful for you specifically — not a repeat of what your VP of Sales has already heard. In your day-to-day, what does the current process actually cost you? Not in money terms — in time, in frustration, in the parts of your job you end up doing on a Friday afternoon that are not really your job.

registerAwareness.context: Presenting to an executive — opening pivot
registerAwareness.example: I will keep this to the business case, because I know your time is limited and you have already been briefed on the operational detail. From a business perspective, the question for you is whether the efficiency gain translates to measurable revenue impact — and I want to give you a specific, defensible answer to that question rather than a projection.

I want to make the procurement process as straightforward as possible. What this means for your team is: a fixed annual cost with no variable charges, a standard data processing agreement that your legal team has approved with other vendors in this category, and a service level agreement with financial penalties for downtime above 0.1%. I can send the full contract terms today so your review starts now rather than at the end of the commercial conversation.

registerAwareness.context: Equipping a champion before an internal meeting
registerAwareness.example: Before the executive review, I want to make sure you have everything you need for the conversations you are going to have without me. I am going to send three things: the CFO one-pager in her language — ROI, risk, and contract structure; the competitive brief for the CEO — two sentences on where your sector is moving and where you sit relative to the companies that have moved early; and the adoption roadmap for the team leads — specifically addressing the concern about previous failed tools. Is there anything else you need for those conversations?

Before we move forward, I want to make sure I have the full picture of who needs to be part of this decision. In most organisations this size, there are stakeholders in the conversation that we have not spoken to yet — sometimes IT, sometimes a senior user, sometimes someone in legal or compliance. Who else needs to see this before you can move to a decision? I would rather surface those conversations now than discover them in the final week.

registerTraps: The most expensive mistake in multi-stakeholder selling is giving every stakeholder the same pitch. The VP of Sales does not need the ROI model — they need the strategic case. The Head of Operations does not need the competitive positioning — they need the adoption roadmap. The procurement team does not need either — they need the contract structure. Same product, four completely different conversations.

What does success look like for you is the most important question you can ask any new stakeholder — because it surfaces their actual definition before you assume it from their job title. A CFO who is focused on cash flow and a CFO who is focused on long-term ROI need completely different conversations, even though they have the same title.

Your champion inside the organisation is having conversations you will never be in. Equip them. Send them the language, the data, and the one-page summary in the format they need for each internal audience. A champion who does not know how to represent your solution internally is not an asset — they are a risk.

Influence is not the same as authority. The senior user who tells the team this is going to be another tool we never actually use can kill a deal the CFO has already approved. Map the influencers, not just the decision-makers — and have the user conversation before the executive conversation, not after.

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Marcus tells Riley that her executive language does not quite connect for him. What has Riley done wrong — and how does she correct it?
options: She has been too informal — she corrects by adopting a more structured, presentation-style format

She has been using the wrong persona — giving an executive proposition to a manager audience; she corrects by resetting to the language of operations, adoption, and team experience rather than strategic impact and ROI
She has not provided enough product detail — she corrects by walking through the features Marcus needs to understand to make a decision
She has been too focused on the problem and not enough on the solution — she corrects by shifting to the outcome story

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Riley suggests starting the rollout with two or three senior users rather than the whole team. What principle is behind this approach?
options: It reduces the implementation cost by limiting the initial licence count
Senior users have formal authority to approve tools on behalf of the team

Influence within a team often travels from senior users downward — if respected voices adopt and endorse the tool, the rest of the team follows; if you start with everyone and hit resistance, the first friction point becomes the defining story
Starting with a smaller group makes the adoption metrics look stronger in the first reporting period

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Why does Riley offer to prepare separate documents for the CFO, the CEO, and the team leads?
options: Because Marcus has limited time and cannot be expected to prepare all the materials himself

Because Marcus is her champion — he will be having conversations about the product in rooms she is not in, and equipping him with the right language and format for each audience is what makes those conversations effective
Because each document needs to be customised with financial projections specific to each stakeholder's budget
Because the company requires all stakeholder communications to go through a single internal advocate to avoid conflicting messages

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Riley goes beyond the obvious stakeholders and includes the Head of IT and senior users. What is she doing?
options: She is creating more stakeholders than necessary to slow the decision and extend the sales cycle

She is identifying influencers alongside formal decision-makers — because the Head of IT's security concerns and the senior users' adoption credibility can each independently stall or kill a deal that the executive team has approved
She is following a standard multi-stakeholder checklist that applies to all enterprise deals regardless of context
She is trying to involve more people so that the decision becomes a group consensus rather than a single executive's call

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Riley tells Marcus that IT and procurement should be engaged now, before anyone asks for it. Why is this important?
options: Because IT and procurement have veto power and must approve before any other stakeholder can move forward
Because surfacing process conversations late in a deal turns minor reviews into blockers; addressing them early means they are resolved before they become obstacles
Because Riley's company policy requires IT and procurement sign-off within the first two meetings of any enterprise sale
Because getting IT and procurement involved early allows Riley to use their approval as social proof with other stakeholders

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What does what does success look like for you accomplish that a standard opening pitch does not?
options: It allows the salesperson to delay the pitch until they have gathered enough information to make it more personalised

It surfaces the specific definition of success this stakeholder holds — before the salesperson assumes it from their job title — allowing the conversation to address what actually matters to them rather than what usually matters to someone in that role
It signals that the salesperson is interested in the prospect's goals rather than their own quota, which builds rapport
It is a standard opening technique that works equally well with all audiences and should be used in every sales conversation

multipleChoiceExercise.question: According to the lesson, why is influence sometimes more important to map than formal authority?
options: Because people with influence often have access to the formal decision-maker that the salesperson does not

Because a person with significant influence — such as a senior user or a Head of IT — can effectively block or undermine a decision that has already been formally approved, making their buy-in as important as the decision-maker's
Because formal authority in large organisations is often delegated, making it difficult to identify who actually holds it
Because mapping influence is faster than mapping the formal hierarchy and gives a quicker path to a decision

multipleChoiceExercise.question: Riley says the CEO conversation should use competitive framing. Why is this different from the CFO conversation?
options: Because the CEO controls a different budget from the CFO and needs a different financial case

Because executives at CEO level are motivated primarily by competitive position and strategic advantage, while CFOs are primarily motivated by financial return and risk — the same product needs to be expressed as a competitive move for the CEO and a financial decision for the CFO
Because the CFO will share the competitive framing with the board, making it inappropriate for that audience
Because CEOs respond to narrative and storytelling while CFOs respond to data, requiring a completely different format

dealClinic.context: Riley has been asked to present to a multi-stakeholder group: the Head of Operations (Marcus), the CFO (Diana), and two senior sales reps (Tom and Priya, the end users). Watch how two salespeople approach this room.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Riley, thank you for coming in. We have Diana from Finance, and Tom and Priya from the sales team who would be the primary users. I wanted everyone in the same room.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson A
transcript.text: Thank you all for your time. I am going to walk you through our platform today — starting with the core features, then the ROI model, and then the implementation timeline. Our platform is a workflow automation tool that integrates with your existing CRM and reduces manual process time by an average of 40% across the sales team. The ROI is typically recovered within two quarters, and our NPS score is 72, which is among the highest in the category.

verdict.explanation: Weak. Salesperson A has delivered a single pitch to an audience with four completely different sets of priorities. The 40% process time reduction is meaningful to Tom and Priya but abstract to Diana, who needs a financial number. The ROI mention is relevant to Diana but premature for Tom and Priya, who have not yet established whether the tool will actually work for them. The NPS score is meaningful to no one in the room without context. Most importantly, Salesperson A has not asked a single question — they have no idea what success looks like for any of the three stakeholder types present.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson B
transcript.text: Thank you — before I say anything, I want to make sure this conversation is actually useful for everyone in the room, because you each have different stakes in this decision. Diana — what does success look like for you in a decision like this? Tom, Priya — same question for you. And Marcus, we have talked about the adoption question — I want to make sure that concern is visible to everyone here before we get into anything else.

verdict.explanation: Strong. Salesperson B opens by surfacing what success means to each person in the room before delivering any content — which means that everything said afterwards can be anchored to what the audience actually cares about. Naming Marcus's adoption concern publicly also signals to Diana and to Tom and Priya that this concern has been heard and will be addressed, rather than buried beneath an ROI slide. The opening takes thirty seconds and positions everything that follows to land with the right person.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Diana's primary concern is the financial case. Tom and Priya want to know if it is going to make their lives harder or easier. And my concern — as Riley knows — is whether we actually adopt this, unlike the last two tools.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson A
transcript.text: Great — I can address all of those. On the financial case, our average ROI is recovered in two quarters. On ease of use, our onboarding rating is 4.8 out of 5. And on adoption, over 90% of our customers have active users six months post-implementation. So I think we cover all three concerns very well.

transcript.speaker: Verdict
transcript.text: Salesperson A — Response to stakeholder concerns

verdict.explanation: Weak. Salesperson A has responded to three different stakeholder concerns with the same device — a statistic. Statistics answer the format of the question without addressing the substance. Diana does not need an average ROI — she needs a specific model for this account. Tom and Priya do not need an onboarding rating — they need to understand what the first month will feel like for them. Marcus does not need an adoption percentage — he needs a rollout structure that addresses the specific pattern of failure he has experienced twice before. The response is efficient but ineffective.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson B
transcript.text: Thank you, Marcus. Let me address each of you directly. Diana — I am going to send you a model built on your specific team size and current process cost, not an average. I want you to be able to stress-test the numbers. Tom, Priya — the way your week would feel different in month one is: the report you currently build on Friday afternoon gets done automatically overnight. Can we do a thirty-minute live session with your actual workflow this week? And Marcus — the adoption structure I am proposing starts with Tom and Priya, not the whole team. If they say it works, the rest of the team follows. If they do not, we do not roll out further until we understand why.

verdict.explanation: Excellent. Salesperson B closes with three separate next steps, each designed for a different stakeholder, each in the language and format that makes sense for that person. Diana gets a model she can stress-test — not a projection. Tom and Priya get a live session with their own workflow — not a demo. Marcus gets a rollout structure that directly addresses his fear of another failed adoption. This is what multi-stakeholder selling looks like at a high level of execution.

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in pairs. For each stakeholder situation, choose the response that best adapts the message to that audience. Discuss your reasoning before clicking.

items.customerLine: A CFO says: What is the business case for this investment?
options: Say: Our platform reduces manual process time by 40% and has an NPS of 72 — our customers consistently report high satisfaction with the ROI they see.

Say: The business case for your specific team is built on three numbers: the current manual process costs your team approximately 880 hours per month. The contract cost is Y. At conservative adoption assumptions, the freed capacity is redirected to pipeline activity and the investment is recovered in one quarter. I will send you a model today that you can stress-test with your own numbers.

Say: From a business perspective, the strategic case is that two companies in your sector started this in Q3 and are now in the compounding phase of the efficiency gain. The window for early-mover advantage is narrowing.
items.explanation: B is correct. A CFO needs a specific, stress-testable financial model — not an average statistic or a category claim. A gives averages and an NPS score that a CFO will dismiss as marketing. C gives a competitive positioning argument that belongs in the CEO conversation, not the CFO's. B gives the specific numbers this organisation can evaluate, offers to send a model the CFO can interrogate, and speaks the language of financial decision-making: cost, contract value, and recovery timeline.

items.customerLine: An end user says: Will this make my job harder or easier?
options: Say: Our onboarding is rated 4.8 out of 5 and our adoption rate at six months is over 90%. Most users find the transition straightforward.

Say: The way your week would feel different in month one is: the report you currently build manually on Friday afternoon gets done automatically overnight. You would still review it — but building it stops being your job. The first two weeks involve learning the system, which takes time. After that, most people describe it as getting hours back rather than adding work. I would rather show you that with your actual workflow than tell you about it.
Say: From a business perspective, the tool frees significant capacity that can be redirected to higher-value activities — which is ultimately what you are there to do.
items.explanation: B is correct. An end user is asking a concrete, personal question — will this make my day better or worse? A gives statistics that do not answer the personal question. C uses executive language that is not how an end user thinks about their job. B translates the product into a specific, day-to-day experience and is honest about the transition cost, which is what makes it credible.

items.customerLine: You have been speaking exclusively to the Head of Operations for three meetings. She says: I think we are close to being ready to move forward.
options: Say: That is great to hear — let me send across the contract and we can work toward a signature by the end of the month.

Say: I am glad to hear that. Before we move to next steps, I want to make sure we have the full picture — who else needs to see this before a decision is made? I would rather surface those conversations now than discover a missing stakeholder when we are trying to close.
Say: Excellent. I will also send a summary of our conversation to your CEO and CFO so they have the full picture — we want to make sure all the right people are informed.
items.explanation: B is correct. A single stakeholder saying we are close to ready is promising — but it does not mean the deal is done. Deals stall most often because a stakeholder who was not identified earlier surfaces a concern at the final stage. B uses this moment to map remaining stakeholders while the Head of Operations is still engaged and the deal has momentum. A moves to contract too fast. C takes the initiative away from the Head of Operations by contacting her seniors directly — which can feel like going around her.

items.customerLine: Your champion messages you: The CFO asked me about the contract terms today and I was not sure how to answer. She wanted to know about what happens if there is downtime.
options: Send your champion a message: The SLA includes financial penalties for any downtime above 0.1%. Let me know if you need anything else.

Send your champion a message: Here is exactly what to say to the CFO on the downtime question: the contract includes a service level agreement with financial penalties for downtime above 0.1% — this means the financial risk of underperformance sits with us, not with your organisation. I am also attaching a one-page SLA summary in plain language she can review directly. Do you want me to join a call with her this week so she can ask questions directly? That might be easier than relaying back and forth.
Send the CFO a direct email: I understand you had some questions about the contract terms — I wanted to reach out directly to answer them rather than passing information through Marcus.
items.explanation: B is correct. Your champion is your advocate in the internal conversation — give them exactly what they need to succeed, not a bare answer they have to translate themselves. B provides the specific language to use, the underlying point that will matter to the CFO, a supporting document, and an offer to join a call if the relay is getting complex. A gives a fact without context or support. C goes around the champion to contact the CFO directly — which can undermine the champion's position and damage the relationship.

profileMatch.instructions: Match each stakeholder profile to the key message they need to hear. Discuss your reasoning before clicking.

profiles.name: Diana — CFO
profiles.description: Diana approved the last three technology purchases and two of them were never fully adopted. She is cautious about new investments and wants to see a specific, stress-testable financial case before she approves anything. She has fifteen minutes.

profiles.name: Tom — Senior Sales Rep
profiles.description: Tom has used four different CRM tools in the last three years, each introduced by management with promises that never materialised. He is the most respected voice in the sales team and his opinion shapes the team's perception of any new tool. He is sceptical.

profiles.name: Elena — Head of Procurement
profiles.description: Elena's job is to protect the organisation from vendor risk. She needs to know that the contract is clean, the data handling is compliant, and there is financial recourse if the vendor underperforms. She does not attend product conversations.

options.label: The investment is recovered within one quarter
options.description: Here is a model built on your specific team size and process cost — not an industry average. The contract cost is X. The freed capacity is Y hours per month. At conservative redirection assumptions, the recovery timeline is one quarter. The SLA includes financial penalties for underperformance, so the downside risk is bounded. You can stress-test every number in this model.

options.label: The way your week feels different
options.description: I am not going to show you a demo. I want to run a live session with your actual workflow this week — your data, your process, your Friday afternoon report. If it does not look meaningfully simpler in the session than it does today, the conversation ends there. I would rather earn your credibility with your own work than with a pre-built demonstration.

options.label: The contract is clean and the risk is bounded
options.description: Here is the full contract, the data processing agreement, and the security documentation — flagged for the three sections that most commonly require review. The SLA includes financial penalties for downtime above 0.1%. The DPA has been approved by legal teams at similar organisations without custom negotiation. I want your review to start today, not at the end of the commercial conversation.

finishTheLine.instructions: Complete each multi-stakeholder response using language from this lesson. Compare your completions before clicking for the suggested answer.

items.customerLine: You are meeting a CFO for the first time. She says: Tell me about the business case.
items.salespersonStart: Before I walk you through the numbers, let me ask: what does success look like
items.suggestedCompletion: for you in a decision like this? I want to make sure the model I show you is built around what you need to evaluate, not around what I think a CFO usually cares about. Some finance leaders want a stress-testable cost model. Others want to see the downside risk bounded. Others want the competitive framing. Which of those is most useful for your conversation?

items.customerLine: A senior user says: I have heard this pitch before. Every tool promises to save time and then adds three new processes.
items.salespersonStart: I hear that — and I am not going to argue with it. The way your week would feel different
items.suggestedCompletion: is something I would rather show you than tell you. Can we do a thirty-minute session this week using your actual workflow — your data, your current Friday process — so you can see for yourself whether it looks simpler or more complex? If the answer is more complex, I want to know that before we go any further. I am not interested in selling you something your team will not actually use.

items.customerLine: You are in a multi-stakeholder meeting and have just finished explaining the product.
items.salespersonStart: Before we talk about next steps — who else needs to see this
items.suggestedCompletion: that is not in the room today? I want to surface any conversations that need to happen before this can move forward, because the most common reason deals stall at the end is a stakeholder who surfaces a concern in the final week that could have been addressed in week two. Procurement, IT, legal, compliance — anyone whose opinion or sign-off matters here?

items.customerLine: Your champion tells you the CEO asked why now in an internal meeting.
items.salespersonStart: Here is exactly what to tell her. From a business perspective,
items.suggestedCompletion: two companies in your sector began this process in Q3. They are now three months into a phase that typically takes six to eight months to fully embed. By the time you start in Q1, the gap is not one quarter — it is closer to two, because the efficiency gain compounds once it is embedded. The why now answer is not that the product is changing or that there is a deadline. It is that the window between starting proactively and starting reactively is shorter than it looks, and it narrows every month.
